text.p: President Bill Clinton used the last presidential inauguration of the 20th century on Monday to declare America a "land of new promise" and call for an end to racial hatred and political bickering.

Clinton, described by aides as obsessed with crafting a second inaugural address that would resonate with the public and earn the respect of historians, spoke slowly and forcefully for 25 minutes as he tried to set a tone for what he hopes to accomplish in the next four years.
"Guided by the ancient vision of a promised land, let us set our sights upon a land of new promise," he said after taking the oath of office at the West Front of the Capitol.

In a speech that echoed the "New Frontier" images of his boyhood idol President John Kennedy and offered inspirational goals rather than specifics on how to attain them, Clinton talked of the ugliness of racism and admitted "the challenge of our past remains the challenge of our future."
"Will we be one nation, one people, with one common destiny -- or not? Will we all come together, or come apart?" he asked the nation.

"The divide of race has been America's constant curse," said Clinton, whose childhood in Arkansas include memories of President Dwight Eisenhower dispatching federal troops to Little Rock to desegregate its schools.
"Each new wave of immigrants gives new targets to old prejudices," he said. "Prejudice and contempt cloaked in the pretense of religious or political convictions are no different.

"These forces have nearly destroyed our nation in the past. They plague us still," said Clinton, who paid tribute to slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., whose famous "I have a dream" speech in 1963 was delivered along the expansive mall from the Capitol at the Lincoln Memorial.

Clinton also vowed to work with the Republican-controlled Congress to cast aside the rancour that has poisoned much of Washington's atmosphere the past two years, noting that "nothing big ever came from being small."
"I ask the members of Congress here to join in that pledge," Clinton said as congressional leaders sat nearby, including House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich.

"The American people returned to office a president of one party and a Congress of another," he said. "Surely they did not do this to advance the politics of petty bickering and extreme partisanship they plainly deplore.

"No, they call on us instead to be repairers of the breach and to move on with America's mission," he said. "America demands and deserves big things from us and nothing big ever came from being small."

White House spopkesman Mike McCurry told reporters after the speech that Clinton believes, based on private conversations with Republican leaders, that "there is a moment here to breach the differences that have existed and he is determined to try to do that."

Clinton, who received a final version of his remarks early in the morning, could be seen making slight revisions up to the last minute. As the formal ceremony was under way he could be seen mentally rehearsing it, at times mouthing the words.

Aides said Clinton offered his vision in broad strokes rather than describing detailed policy proposals -- preferring to save that for his Feb. 4 State of the Union address to a joint session of Congress.
